 Meet the clerks who steward Wisconsin’s elections
 Election integrity is front and center ahead of the midterms
 By Sara Gabler 
 October 29, 2026 
 Download 
 Absentee ballots during a count at the Wisconsin Center, Nov. 8, 2022, in Milwaukee. Morry Gash/AP Photo, File 
 Ahead of Election Day, Dunn County Clerk Andrew Mercil and Village of Shorewood Clerk Toya Harrell joined “The Lee Rayburn Show” to discuss how they keep Wisconsin’s elections safe and secure. 
 Wisconsin’s elections are administered by 72 county clerks and roughly 1,850 municipal clerks. It takes a lot of coordination and cooperation between offices to make this happen. Mercil believes this is a strength.
 “Wisconsin is more than just beer and cheese. We have excellent elections. One of the strong suits of the decentralized nature of our elections that are run at the county and the municipal level is that it’s really hard to try to do anything to influence the election because everything is handled between the 1,850 municipalities across the state of Wisconsin,” Mercil said.

 Wisconsin also participates in the Electronic Registration Information Center , which is a national system that compares voter data. Twenty seven states currently participate in this program.
 “If a voter is voting here in Wisconsin and they tried to vote somewhere else in the same election, the systems would talk to each other and notify them that it’s been happening,” Mercil explained.
 There are also local checks and balances, Harrell explained. After the polls are closed, election inspectors sign off on results and then certify them on a call-in sheet. These results are reported to the county where, in the days after the election, the results are certified. 
 “We make sure that the numbers that are put on the webpage have been checked and rechecked, and sometimes re-rechecked,” Harrell said.
 Ahead of Election Day
 This is the fourth election that Harrell and Mercil have administered this year, and their work begins weeks and months ahead of Election Day.
 Harrell makes sure that there are adequate supplies like forms for her chief inspectors; that all signage is up to date with the proper notices; that the election poll book, called Badger Books , is loaded; that there are emergency plans for staff outages; and that meals for her poll workers are ordered ahead of time. 
 Mercil and Harrell have been busy training their teams on election security and deescalation to make sure that polling places are “nice and neutral” ground. This includes making poll workers aware of who is and isn’t allowed to be at the polls in order to protect voter safety.
 As some express concern over possible federal agents appearing at polling places, Mercil said law enforcement should be at a polling place only to carry out their law enforcement duties, such as if they are called by a chief inspector. 
 While registered election observers are permitted, observers should not engage with voters or take video.
 “We really take a lot of pride in Article I, Section 4, Clause 1 [of the Constitution], the Election Clause , that dictates that states run the elections,” Mercil said. 
 Democracy at work
 One difference between municipal and county clerks is that the county clerks are elected in partisan elections. Municipal clerks can be appointed or elected in a nonpartisan election.
 “But regardless of my colleagues who are Republicans and Democrats, we don’t run Republican elections or Democratic elections. We run the way the election laws are dictated in Wisconsin,” Mercil said.
 If you are worried about the integrity of your ballot, Harrell invites you to attend a public testing of voting tabulation machines or simply talk to your local clerk. 
 Harrell said she’s seen a surge of poll workers who she calls superheroes. 
 “They really are just everyday people coming together for the common good. They really do put themselves out there to ensure safety, to make sure that our polling locations are welcoming, and to make sure that the elector feels at peace,” Harrell said. “The bottom line is: We are there to make sure that their vote counts.”
 And at the end of the day, “the people that are working the polls are our neighbors,” Mercil said.
 Casting your ballot
 If you have not returned your absentee ballot, it is too late to drop it in the mail. Mercil and Harrell recommend dropping your ballot off to your municipal clerk’s office, in a drop box, during in-person absentee voting or at your polling place on Election Day.
 If you’re planning to cast your ballot on Nov. 3, be sure that you have an acceptable photo ID (such as a passport or Wisconsin-issued ID) before you head to your polling place . 
 You can even register to vote on Election Day at your polling place. Bring proof of residence such as a utility bill or bank statement and an acceptable photo ID.
 Find out how to vote on Nov. 3 at myvote.wi.gov . And find more information about candidates and key issues at  WPR’s 2026 General Election Voter Guide .
